lessonTitle: Torsional Vibration of Single and Two-Inertia Systems

blocks.text: A lab technician twists the free end of a slender steel rod with a heavy disc clamped to it, lets go, and the disc swings back and forth about the rod axis like a pendulum. The rod is the spring and the disc is the inertia. Shaft-and-disc assemblies in every drivetrain ring in exactly the same way.

blocks.markdown: **Torsional vibration** is oscillation of rotating inertias about the shaft axis, with the shaft acting as a torsional spring. The quantities mirror those of linear vibration: displacement $x$ becomes angle $\theta$ (rad), mass $m$ becomes polar mass moment of inertia $I$ (kg m$^2$), force becomes torque $T$ (N m), and stiffness $k$ becomes torsional stiffness $k_t$ (N m/rad). The equation of motion of a single inertia on a massless shaft, with no damping and no applied torque, is $I\ddot{\theta}+k_t\theta=0$.

blocks.title: Torsional stiffness of a circular shaft
blocks.text: A shaft of length $L$ (m), shear modulus $G$ (Pa) and polar second moment of area $J$ (m$^4$) twists by $\theta=TL/(GJ)$ under torque $T$. Hence its torsional stiffness is $k_t=T/\theta=GJ/L$. For a solid circular section of diameter $d$, $J=\pi d^4/32$; for a hollow section with outer and inner diameters $d_o$ and $d_i$, $J=\pi(d_o^4-d_i^4)/32$.

blocks.caption: Shaft stiffness and one-disc natural frequency (rad/s and Hz)

blocks.title: A disc on a shaft
blocks.prompt: A solid steel shaft of diameter 30 mm and length 0.6 m (G = 80 GPa) is fixed at one end and carries a uniform disc of mass 20 kg and radius 0.2 m on its free end. Neglect the shaft inertia. Find the torsional natural frequency.

steps.text: Polar second moment of area of the shaft.
Disc inertia for a uniform solid disc, I = (1/2) m R^2.

blocks.answer: k_t = 10603 N m/rad, I = 0.40 kg m^2, omega_n = 162.8 rad/s = 25.91 Hz.

blocks.markdown: **Two discs on one shaft.** Now put inertias $I_1$ and $I_2$ at the two ends of a shaft of stiffness $k_t$, with no external support (a free-free system). Let $\theta_1,\theta_2$ be the disc angles. The shaft torque is $k_t(\theta_2-\theta_1)$, giving $I_1\ddot{\theta}_1=k_t(\theta_2-\theta_1)$ and $I_2\ddot{\theta}_2=-k_t(\theta_2-\theta_1)$. Adding them shows $I_1\ddot\theta_1+I_2\ddot\theta_2=0$, so for a vibration mode (both discs $\propto\cos\omega t$) $I_1\theta_1=-I_2\theta_2$: the discs move in **opposite directions**, with the larger inertia moving the smaller angle. Subtracting the equations gives $\ddot\theta_2-\ddot\theta_1=-k_t(1/I_1+1/I_2)(\theta_2-\theta_1)$. The other root of the characteristic equation is $\omega=0$, the rigid-body rotation.

blocks.caption: Two-disc natural frequency and distances from each disc to the node

blocks.markdown: **The node.** Because $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ have opposite signs, the twist angle varies linearly along the shaft and passes through zero at a section called the **node**, which stays at rest while the discs swing either side. If $l_1$ and $l_2$ are the distances from disc 1 and disc 2 to the node, $l_1+l_2=L$, and the angle amplitudes are in proportion $\theta_1/\theta_2=-l_1/l_2$. Comparing with $I_1\theta_1=-I_2\theta_2$ gives $l_1/l_2=I_2/I_1$, so $l_1=LI_2/(I_1+I_2)$. The node lies **closer to the larger inertia**. Each disc then behaves like a single disc on a shaft of length $l_i$: $\omega_n^2=GJ/(l_1I_1)=GJ/(l_2I_2)$.

blocks.title: Free-free two-disc system
blocks.prompt: A steel shaft of diameter 40 mm and length 1.0 m (G = 80 GPa) carries a disc of inertia 0.5 kg m^2 at one end and a disc of inertia 1.5 kg m^2 at the other. Find the natural frequency and the node position.

steps.text: Natural frequency from the two-disc formula.
Node distance from disc 1 (the lighter one): the node divides the shaft in the inverse ratio of the inertias.
Check using disc 2 alone on a shaft of length l_2.

blocks.answer: omega_n = 231.6 rad/s (36.85 Hz); the node is 0.75 m from the lighter disc and 0.25 m from the heavier one.

items: Compute each disc inertia (for a solid disc $I=\tfrac12mR^2$, in kg m$^2$).
Find the node from $l_1=LI_2/(I_1+I_2)$; check with $\omega_n^2=k_tL/(l_1I_1)$.

blocks.title: Limit check
blocks.text: If $I_2\to\infty$, the second disc cannot move and acts like a rigid wall, so the two-disc frequency must tend to the one-disc value $\sqrt{k_t/I_1}$: $k_t(I_1+I_2)/(I_1I_2)\to k_t/I_1$. The node moves to disc 2. A formula that fails this check has been remembered wrongly.

blocks.title: Neglecting the shaft's own inertia
blocks.text: The formulas assume a massless shaft. A real shaft adds some inertia, which lowers the true natural frequency slightly. The estimate is acceptable when the shaft inertia is a small fraction (below about 10 to 20 per cent, typical guidance) of the disc inertia.

points: A circular shaft is a torsional spring with $k_t=GJ/L$ and $J=\pi d^4/32$ for a solid section.
One disc on a shaft: $\omega_n=\sqrt{k_t/I}$ in rad/s.
Two discs on a free-free shaft: $\omega_n^2=k_t(I_1+I_2)/(I_1I_2)$; the discs oscillate in antiphase about a node at $l_1=LI_2/(I_1+I_2)$ from disc 1.
The node is nearer the larger inertia, and the two-disc result tends to the one-disc result as one inertia becomes very large.

questions.stem: A solid circular shaft is replaced by another of the same material and length but twice the diameter. Its torsional stiffness changes by a factor of

distractorRationale.a: Correct: The polar second moment of area is J = pi d^4/32, so doubling d multiplies J, and therefore k_t = GJ/L, by 2^4 = 16.
distractorRationale.b: Stiffness depends on the fourth power of the diameter, not the first.
distractorRationale.c: That would result from the square of the diameter, which applies to the area.
distractorRationale.d: That would result from the cube of the diameter.

questions.explanation: The polar second moment of area is J = pi d^4/32, so doubling d multiplies J, and therefore k_t = GJ/L, by 2^4 = 16. A small change in diameter has a large effect on torsional stiffness.

questions.stem: A solid steel shaft has diameter 25 mm and length 0.4 m, with a shear modulus of 79 GPa. Find its torsional stiffness in N m/rad.
questions.explanation: The polar second moment of area is pi d^4/32 = pi x (0.025)^4/32 = 3.8350 x 10^{-8} m^4. The stiffness is G J/L = 7.900 x 10^10 x 3.8350 x 10^{-8}/0.4 = 7574 N m/rad.

questions.stem: Two discs of different inertia are joined by a free-free shaft and vibrate in their fundamental torsional mode. Where is the node?

options.text: At the midpoint of the shaft, whatever the inertias
Nearer the disc with the larger inertia, at distances from the discs in inverse proportion to their inertias
At the disc with the smaller inertia
The system has no node, because both discs move together

questions.correctOptionText: Nearer the disc with the larger inertia, at distances from the discs in inverse proportion to their inertias

distractorRationale.a: The midpoint is correct only for equal inertias.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: The condition I_1 theta_1 = -I_2 theta_2 means the larger inertia has the smaller angle, and the angle varies linearly along the shaft through zero.
distractorRationale.c: The smaller disc swings through the larger angle, so it is furthest from the node.
distractorRationale.d: The discs move in opposite directions, so a node must lie between them.

questions.explanation: The condition I_1 theta_1 = -I_2 theta_2 means the larger inertia has the smaller angle, and the angle varies linearly along the shaft through zero. The zero crossing therefore lies closer to the larger inertia, at l_1 = L I_2/(I_1 + I_2).

questions.stem: A disc of polar inertia 0.08 kg m^2 is carried on a shaft of torsional stiffness 4500 N m/rad, the other end of the shaft being rigidly fixed. Neglecting the shaft inertia, find the natural frequency in Hz.
questions.explanation: The angular frequency is sqrt(k_t/I) = sqrt(4500/0.08) = 237.2 rad/s. Dividing by 2 pi gives 37.75 Hz.

questions.stem: A free-free steel shaft of diameter 20 mm and length 0.5 m (G = 80 GPa) carries discs of inertia 0.8 kg m^2 and 0.2 kg m^2 at its ends. Find the torsional natural frequency in Hz.

A turbine of inertia 3.0 kg m^2 and a generator of inertia 1.0 kg m^2 are joined by a uniform free-free shaft 2.0 m long. In the fundamental torsional mode, the node lies at what distance from the turbine?

distractorRationale.a: That is the distance from the generator; the node lies nearer the heavier disc.
distractorRationale.b: The midpoint applies only to equal inertias.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: The node divides the shaft in inverse proportion to the inertias: l_turbine = L I_gen/(I_turb + I_gen) = 2.0 x 1.0/4.0 = 0.50 m.
distractorRationale.d: That is the inertia ratio times the length, which is not the node distance formula.

questions.explanation: The node divides the shaft in inverse proportion to the inertias: l_turbine = L I_gen/(I_turb + I_gen) = 2.0 x 1.0/4.0 = 0.50 m. It is closer to the heavy turbine.

questions.stem: When the inertia of the shaft itself is neglected in calculating the torsional natural frequency of a disc on a shaft, the calculated value is

options.text: slightly lower than the true value
exactly equal to the true value
slightly higher than the true value, since the neglected shaft inertia would lower the frequency

questions.correctOptionText: slightly higher than the true value, since the neglected shaft inertia would lower the frequency

distractorRationale.a: Adding inertia to a system reduces its frequency, so ignoring it overestimates the frequency.
distractorRationale.b: The shaft has inertia, which does change the frequency, though only a little when the discs are heavy.
distractorRationale.c: The estimate is close to the true value when the shaft inertia is small.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: A real shaft carries distributed inertia that adds to the effective inertia, so the true natural frequency is lower than sqrt(k_t/I).

questions.explanation: A real shaft carries distributed inertia that adds to the effective inertia, so the true natural frequency is lower than sqrt(k_t/I). The massless-shaft estimate is therefore an upper bound, close to the true value when the disc dominates.

questions.stem: Derive the natural frequency of a two-disc free-free torsional system from the equations of motion, and show how the position of the node follows from the mode.
markingGuide: Equations: I1 theta1'' = k_t (theta2 - theta1) and I2 theta2'' = -k_t (theta2 - theta1)
Adding: I1 theta1'' + I2 theta2'' = 0, so in a vibrating mode I1 theta1 = -I2 theta2 (antiphase)
Subtract after dividing by the inertias to get (theta2 - theta1)'' = -k_t (1/I1 + 1/I2)(theta2 - theta1)
Angle varies linearly along the shaft: theta1/theta2 = -l1/l2, so l1/l2 = I2/I1
l1 = L I2/(I1 + I2): node is nearer the larger inertia
Check: each side behaves as a single disc on a shaft of length l_i: omega_n^2 = GJ/(l_i I_i)
questions.explanation: The antiphase condition follows from momentum balance, and the frequency from the relative twist. The node is where the linear twist distribution passes through zero.

questions.stem: A student calculates the natural frequency of a two-disc shaft and finds that when one disc is made enormously heavier, the answer does not approach the one-disc result sqrt(k_t/I_1). Explain how you would check the two-disc formula in this limit and where the node should lie.
markingGuide: Take I2 tending to infinity in omega^2 = k_t (I1 + I2)/(I1 I2)
So omega tends to sqrt(k_t/I1), the fixed-end single-disc result
Node position l1 = L I2/(I1 + I2) tends to L: the node moves to the heavy disc, which acts as a fixed end
A formula giving something else, such as k_t/I1 + k_t/I2 without a square root or a swapped inertia, has been misremembered
Physical argument: a very heavy disc hardly moves, so it acts like a wall
questions.explanation: The two-disc formula can be written k_t(1/I1 + 1/I2), which reduces to k_t/I1 when I2 is very large. The node migrates to the heavy disc, which then acts as a fixed end.

questions.stem: For a given shaft material and diameter, increasing the shaft length increases its torsional stiffness.
questions.explanation: The torsional stiffness is k_t = GJ/L, so it is inversely proportional to the length. A longer shaft twists more under the same torque and so has a lower natural frequency.
